name: Mewing appliances
lead: Mewing appliances are oral devices, including palate-expanding plates, mouthpieces and tongue-posture aids, marketed to accompany 'mewing', the practice of resting the whole tongue against the roof of the mouth with the lips sealed and breathing through the nose. Mewing is named after the British orthodontist John Mew and belongs to orthotropics, his theory that tongue, lip and breathing posture guide facial growth.[1]

Proponents claim sustained correct posture can produce a more forward jaw, sharper jawline and improved midface and airway. Orthodontic organisations cited in an encyclopedic summary state that mewing cannot reliably reshape the jaw or correct bite problems, and the American Association of Orthodontists has cautioned against forcing unnatural tongue positions.[1] A 2019 article in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery examined mewing as a social media alternative to orthognathic surgery, and a 2026 piece in the Journal of Clinical Orthodontics addressed the trend.[3][4]

No randomized or controlled trial of over-the-counter mewing appliances in adults has been published in the sources reviewed here. The closest research concerns clinician-supervised orthodontic and orthotropic treatment, mostly in children, and case reports in adults.

paras: Products sold under the mewing banner include flexible palate plates and mouthpieces meant to hold the tongue or lips in position, tongue trainers, and palatal expanders. These are distinct from prescription orthodontic expanders fitted by a clinician. The central practice they support, tongue posture, requires no device at all, and a tracking app and tutorials are promoted by the Mew family's circle.[1]

John Mew qualified as a surgeon in 1953 and moved into orthodontics in 1965, later formulating the 'Tropic Premise', a view that malocclusion arises mainly from environmental posture rather than genetics.[1] According to Grokipedia, he founded the London School of Facial Orthotropics in 1983 and described an appliance approach called Bioblock therapy.[1] His son Mike Mew promoted orthotropics from the 2010s, and the practice gained global attention through YouTube and TikTok.[1]

Grokipedia reports that both Mews faced professional regulatory consequences, including a 2017 General Dental Council licence revocation for John Mew and erasure of Mike Mew from the dental register in 2024, while Mike Mew continues to advocate orthotropics.[1] These accounts come from a single AI-generated source and should be read as reported rather than confirmed here.

Orthotropic theory holds that tongue pressure on the palate and a lip seal influence how the maxilla and mandible grow, so that correct posture encourages forward rather than downward growth. John Mew published a 1992 paper arguing that orthotropic guidance in children could influence oropharyngeal development and ear ventilation.[6] Primate experiments by Egil Harvold are cited by orthotropics supporters as background for posture-driven malocclusion.[1]

Mainstream orthodontic view, as summarised, is that such effects are plausible in growing children under appropriate treatment but that evidence of skeletal change in adults from tongue posture or consumer appliances is lacking.[1]

A twin study published in 2007 compared 12 identical twin pairs, one twin treated with fixed orthodontic appliances and the other with orthotropic treatment; 12 lay judges rated most conventionally treated twins as less attractive after treatment and most orthotropically treated twins as improved. The study came from the orthotropics literature and was small.[2] A 2009 case report described condylar bone formation and symptom resolution in a 30-year-old man with temporomandibular disorder who wore a clinician-prescribed hard acrylic splint that advanced the mandible 2.5 mm; the authors noted that one case cannot establish causation.[5] A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis examined mouth breathing and atypical swallowing.[7]
None of these assessed over-the-counter mewing appliances in adults.

The American Association of Orthodontists has cautioned that forcing unnatural tongue positions could lead to tooth misalignment, bite problems or speech changes and recommends professional supervision.[1] Ill-fitting oral devices can also cause discomfort or jaw-joint strain, according to dental advice generally.

A 2025 qualitative analysis of 8,072 comments on a large looksmaxxing forum found that the community encouraged men to substantially alter their bodies, with mewing named among practices alongside leg lengthening surgery, and argued that the community's culture is harmful to participants' health.[8] Mewing is among the best-known terms in looksmaxxing vocabulary.

No studies found on consumer mewing appliances. Related human research includes a 12-pair twin study of orthotropic versus fixed-appliance treatment,[2] an adult splint case report,[5] and a systematic review of mouth breathing and atypical swallowing.[7] Reviews and commentary in oral surgery and orthodontic journals discuss the trend rather than report trials.[3][4]

lore.intro: Mewing is among the most-discussed topics on looksmax.org, where threads range from reports of visible change to reports of no change or of perceived harm, and where palate expanders are often discussed alongside tongue posture.[9][11][13][14]

claims.claim: Mewing produces forward maxillary and chin growth, including in adults.
claims.believers: Threads titled "mewing works and heres how to do it" and "mewing crazy results of forward growth in 20 year old patient of john mew" present before-and-after accounts of forward growth.[14][11]
claims.experts: A 2007 twin study of 12 pairs from the orthotropics literature found lay judges rated most orthotropically treated twins as improved, and the article's sources describe it as small.[2] Orthodontic organisations cited in an encyclopedic summary state mewing cannot reliably reshape the jaw, and no trial of mewing in adults has been published in the sources reviewed.[1]

claims.claim: Mewing yields at most 1-2 mm in the teen years and mostly acts through a temporary hyoid lift.
claims.believers: One looksmax.org post says mewing at ages 14-17 will do little, to "expect 1-2mm at most," and that it temporarily lifts the hyoid bone for a sharper jawline; another poster, who says they mewed from ages 13-14 and still has a recessed midface, writes that mewing may be "cope."[10][9]
claims.experts: Mainstream orthodontic opinion, as summarised, holds that posture effects are plausible in growing children under supervised treatment but that evidence of skeletal change in adults is lacking.[1] The sources reviewed contain no measurement of a hyoid-lift effect on jawline appearance.

claims.claim: Mewing combined with a palatal expander or MSE improves the midface.
claims.believers: A thread titled "mewing and palatal expander" and the posting of a user with a narrow palate who plans MSE then braces reflect the common pairing of tongue posture with expansion.[12][9]
claims.experts: The article's sources note that clinician-fitted expanders differ from over-the-counter mewing appliances, and no randomized or controlled trial of consumer mewing appliances in adults has been published.[1]

claims.claim: Mewing can damage the face or teeth.
claims.believers: A thread titled "mewing ruined my face" reports perceived harm from the practice.[13]
claims.experts: The American Association of Orthodontists has cautioned that forcing unnatural tongue positions could lead to tooth misalignment, bite problems or speech changes.[1]

claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread titled "mewing lowers anxiety scientific study proof" asserts that a scientific study supports an anxiety benefit.[15]
claims.experts: None of the sources reviewed for this article examined mewing and anxiety; the cited reviews address jaw growth, mouth breathing and swallowing.[3][4][7]
